newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korea, ADB may begin entry talks this year.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea, ADB may begin entry talks this year.

text.p: Impoverished North Korea may begin talks this year on membership in the Asian Development Bank (ADB), which offers cheap loans to the region's poorest nations, an ADB spokesman said on Thursday.
"Substantive discussions have not yet commenced. They may start in the second half of this year," Robert Salamon told a news conference in Seoul.
"The bank has received indications North Korea is interested in commencing a dialogue with a view to becoming a member of the ADB," he said.

North Korea is desperate for foreign capital to try to revive its Stalinist-style economy, which has been in ruins since the collapse of the former Soviet Union robbed the country of a major source of aid and investment.

Pyongyang has been totally cut off from international financial markets since it stopped paying interest on its foreign debt in 1984. According to South Korean figures, Pyongyang's foreign debt exceeds $10 billion.
"Poverty reduction is a major strategic objective of the ADB. In light of that, any country which joins the bank and which has a serious problem would be eligible for emergency loans," Salamon said.
North Korea officially applied for membership of the Manila-based institution in 1992, but the bank decided its entry bid was premature.
Salamon said there had been "sporadic expressions of interest" by North Korea since then.
North Korea was one of a handful of countries seeking membership in the ADB, whose largest donors include Japan and the United States, he said.

Salamon said North Korea already met one condition of membership, which states that all members should belong to the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific, which is part of the United Nations Development Programme.
The other condition was that there must be a "favourable consensus" among the ADB's 56 members.
A formal application by North Korea would be referred for discussion to the ADB.
Salamon cautioned that "these discussions can last for months and months".
Interest in trading in North Korean debt -- once worthless paper -- has been picking up on hopes that the country will be gradually brought into the international community.
Such hopes have been heightened by diplomatic activity aimed at enticing Pyongyang to join four-way peace talks with South Korea, the United States and China.

U.S. and South Koren officials held inconclusive talks with Pyongyang representatives in New York on Wednesday, during which North Korea indicated it would give its answer on whether it would participate in the peace talks.
However, all sides reported progress and said they hoped to settle the issue on Friday.
The talks are aimed at replacing an armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War with a permanent peace.
